meta.design: One row per guard family, written from the source text before the kernel is run. The golden set measures deciding; this set measures refusing for the right reason, with controls so a guard that refuses everything cannot pass.

probes.text: Folic acid 200 mcg daily prevents neural tube defects.
probes.note: E087 states 400 mcg; 200 mcg is a different dose, so its stance is out of scope.

probes.text: Folic acid 800 mcg daily prevents neural tube defects.
probes.note: Same card, a different amount. A higher dose is not entailed by a card about 400 mcg.

probes.text: Vitamin D above 40,000 IU per day is not recommended.
probes.note: E088 gives the magnitude as 4,000 IU; 40,000 IU is ten times that, not a rounding.

probes.text: Folic acid 400 mcg daily prevents neural tube defects in men.
probes.note: The card is population-unmarked and the claim narrows to men, so the scope guard refuses.

probes.text: Folic acid 400 mcg daily prevents neural tube defects.
probes.note: Control: same dose, same subject, and the card states it.

probes.text: A hand sanitizer that contains 40% alcohol cleans hands well.
probes.note: The poisoning card is about a harm, not about whether the product cleans; E090's efficacy threshold is not reachable from a 40% claim, so nothing decides it.

probes.text: A hand sanitizer that contains 60% alcohol cleans hands well.
probes.note: Control: 60% is the card's own threshold.

probes.text: Coffee prevents cancer.
probes.note: A card that coffee causes cancer cannot decide the opposite relation.

probes.text: Coffee causes cancer.
probes.note: Control: the relation matches the card, and the source refutes it.

probes.text: Vitamin C cures the flu.
probes.note: Curing is not preventing: the vitamin C cards are about colds, and none states a cure.

probes.text: Alcohol gel rubbed into the hands stops influenza from spreading.
probes.note: An object word (spread) must not make a vaccine-side-effect card decide a prevention claim.

probes.text: Coffee causes cancer in children.
probes.note: The card is about adults; a paediatric version is a different proposition.

probes.text: MSG causes headaches in pregnant women.
probes.note: A pregnancy card cannot decide a general MSG claim and vice versa.

probes.text: Vaccination against flu is unsafe for pregnant women.
probes.note: Control: the eligibility card is exactly about this population.

probes.text: A baby's immune system is overwhelmed by vaccines.
probes.note: Control: the card is about infants and refutes it.

probes.text: Flu vaccines are safe.
probes.note: A refuted side-effect claim is not proof of general safety; the corpus has no safety card.

probes.text: Alcohol hand sanitizer is safe for children.
probes.note: No card states paediatric safety, so the broad attribute cannot be decided.

probes.text: Taking more than 4,000 IU of vitamin D each day is not advised.
probes.note: A prohibition is not a logical negation: the upper-limit card supports it.

probes.text: Taking more than 4,000 IU of vitamin D per day is recommended.
probes.note: Inverted control: the same card refutes the positive form.

probes.text: Our planet is not round.
probes.note: Polarity flips the supporting card into a refutation.

probes.text: It is not true that the Earth is flat.
probes.note: One negation inverts the refuting card back into support.

probes.text: The Earth is round and the Earth is flat.
probes.note: A contradictory compound splits; the first atom keeps its own verdict (second is refuted).

probes.text: Antibiotics can cure both the common cold and influenza.
probes.note: A coordinated object stays whole; the claim is not truncated to cold.

probes.text: Taking more than 4,000 IU of vitamin D a day is not advised.
probes.note: A thousands separator belongs to the number, not to a clause boundary.

probes.text: 4,000 IU of vitamin D per day is not recommended for adults.
probes.note: The card gives no adult-specific statement, so the narrowed claim refuses.

probes.text: The Earth is round.
probes.note: Plain control.

probes.text: A flu shot infects you with the flu.
probes.note: Plain control.

probes.text: Antibiotics can treat a common cold.
probes.note: Plain control.

probes.text: Soap and water handwashing prevents respiratory and diarrheal infections.
probes.note: Plain control for the hygiene card.

probes.text: Eating carrots supports eye health.
probes.note: Plain control for the vision card.

probes.text: Antibiotics cause side effects.
probes.note: E092 reads "antibiotics have no side effects", so a positive restatement of the opposite must land supported. Checking only the claim's own negation would report refuted.

probes.text: Antibiotics do not cause side effects.
probes.note: The claim repeats the card, so the negation must not be applied twice.

probes.text: Antibiotics never have side effects.
probes.note: E093 says side effects are rare in children: rare is not never, so it is excluded instead of lending support to an absolute.

probes.text: Smoking always causes lung cancer.
probes.note: Control: the card's own statement is absolute enough for an absolute claim.

probes.text: Cancer causes death.
probes.note: Cancer is E086's object, not its subject: coffee causing cancer says nothing about what cancer causes, so the chain link may not be borrowed from the card.

probes.text: Smoking causes lung cancer.
probes.note: Control: the card's subject is the claim's subject, so it still decides.

probes.text: Dry indoor air may encourage coronavirus spread
probes.note: E122 asserts that exposure to air spreads a tumour. Air and spread are the only shared words; the conditions are different, so the card cannot decide a coronavirus claim. This exact pair was answered refuted on the dev slice before the outcome vocabulary knew the word tumour.

probes.text: Exposure to air makes a tumour spread
probes.note: The control for H37: the same card still decides the claim it is actually about. A guard that refused this as well would be a blanket refusal, not a comparison.

probes.text: Cold weather kills the coronavirus
probes.note: The second control: coronavirus and covid are now one condition class, so the weather cards must keep deciding weather claims. Merging the two words was required by this fix; refusing these as well would have paid for precision with coverage that already worked.
